title: Mexico’s Homicides Are Falling, but a Broader Violence Crisis Persists
gist: Mexico under Sheinbaum and security chief García Harfuch has cut daily homicides ~51% (Sep 2024 to Jul 2026) via a confrontational, intelligence-led, US-aligned strategy, but extortion, 135,000+ disappearances, forced recruitment and pretrial-detention overload persist. The author argues gains are fragile unless security is regionalized (Coahuila model) and Morena confronts criminal-political ties before the June 2027 elections.

insights.claim: Mexico's daily average of intentional homicides fell 51% between September 2024 and July 2026 per government SESNSP data, and INEGI also shows a national decline despite methodological differences.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: A durable homicide decline lowers Mexico country-risk and nearshoring security premia; track SESNSP vs INEGI divergence for data-quality risk.
insights.locator: The figure compares September 2024 with July 2026

insights.claim: Sheinbaum and security secretary Omar García Harfuch quietly converted López Obrador's 'hugs, not bullets' policy into direct confrontation with organized crime, targeting 'violence generators' and cartels' financial and logistical operators.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: Policy regime shift toward enforcement and financial targeting implies more AML scrutiny and cartel-finance pressure on Mexican banks and businesses.
insights.quote: They quietly converted former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s “hugs, not bullets” policy into a strategy of direct confrontation with organized crime.

insights.claim: The Mexican government reports that the daily average of 'high-impact' crimes in 2026 is 54% below 2018, and independent scholars broadly agree on a significant reduction while flagging possible statistical errors, mismanagement and manipulation.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: Headline crime statistics are directionally credible but carry manipulation risk; discount official figures somewhat.

insights.claim: From October 2024 to July 2026 Mexican security forces arrested 63,000 people linked to crime, seized 32,824 firearms and 519 tons of drugs, and destroyed 2,725 clandestine labs.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: Enforcement intensity metrics show supply-side pressure on cartels, relevant to US fentanyl politics and bilateral trade negotiations.

insights.claim: Mexico's relative crime-fighting success and intensified alignment with the United States have helped contain Trump's pressure and restrain MAGA hardliners advocating unilateral US military action in Mexico.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: Continued security cooperation is a key hedge against US tariff or military escalation on Mexico; a reversal in crime data would raise that tail risk.

insights.claim: Extortion ('criminal taxation') is now one of Mexico's most persistent and fastest-growing crimes, hitting everyone from street vendors to major businesses, and drug seizures and lab destruction do little to curb it.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: Extortion is a direct operating cost for companies in Mexico (retail, logistics, consumer); falling homicides do not imply lower business security costs.

insights.claim: Mexico has more than 135,000 missing people, with a growing share forcibly recruited by criminal organizations as hitmen, sex workers, logistics operators and messengers.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: Forced recruitment signals cartels' continued labor and territorial capacity despite leadership decapitation; a reputational/ESG risk in affected regions.
insights.quote: Mexico now has more than 135,000 missing people.

insights.claim: Sheinbaum continues to downplay disappearances and forced labor and omitted them entirely from her second presidential address.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: Government messaging may overstate security progress; rely on independent sources for regional risk.

insights.claim: Arrests are not convictions: since 2018 Morena has aggressively broadened mandatory pretrial detention, and about 102,000 Mexicans are incarcerated awaiting resolution of their cases.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: Rule-of-law weakness persists under strong enforcement numbers, relevant to institutional-quality assessments of Mexico.
insights.quote: To start, arrests are not convictions.
insights.locator: To start, arrests are not convictions.

insights.claim: Mass automatic incarceration hits marginalized communities hardest and risks mainly catching replaceable street-level operators rather than criminal middle and upper management.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: Arrest-count headlines may overstate damage to cartel organizational capacity.

insights.claim: Excessive centralization is the key weakness of Sheinbaum's security strategy; México Evalúa warns the national drop in violence will be hard to sustain without stronger regional police and prosecutors.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: Watch for federal funding/professionalization of state police as a signal of durable security gains.
insights.locator: These problems signal a key weakness

insights.claim: Violence is diverging by state: Coahuila, Querétaro and Tlaxcala show sharp declines while Colima, Guerrero, Michoacán and Sinaloa face intensifying or persistent violence.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: Location-specific risk: favor Coahuila/Querétaro-type states for nearshoring footprints; treat Sinaloa, Michoacán, Guerrero, Colima (port of Manzanillo region) as elevated risk.
insights.quote: For residents of those states, the “national reduction” in violence may feel like little more than a statistical fiction.

insights.claim: The federal government can strengthen and professionalize weaker, corruption-prone local police without ceding leadership or oversight, rebutting the common objection to regionalizing security.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: Policy path toward hybrid federal-state models could be a positive catalyst for regional risk.
insights.locator: A common objection to regionalizing security policy

insights.claim: Coahuila's pacification from Los Zetas control in the early 2010s combined federal firepower with a strengthened state police targeting top leadership until the group's economic base and command collapsed, plus a private-sector pact against money laundering.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: A replicable template: federal-state coordination plus business AML pacts; look for its adoption in hotspots as a leading indicator of improvement.
insights.locator: Coahuila offers an often-overlooked success story.

insights.claim: Sheinbaum and Morena have gone easy on officials suspected of criminal ties, prioritizing ruling-coalition cohesion over confronting criminal groups' political influence.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: Political protection of criminal networks caps how far security gains can go; key governance risk for Mexico.
insights.locator: This kind of federal-state cooperation will be vital.

insights.claim: Tightened vetting of candidates for major offices in the June 2027 elections, without a party purge, is probably not enough while criminal political protection rackets and impunity remain intact.
insights.speaker: JACQUES COSTE
insights.so_what: Watch June 2027 candidate lists and any cartel-linked candidacies as a test of political will.
insights.locator: It appears that Sheinbaum is opting for a middle path
